body: Some background, since someone has to provide it. KNX is the wiring standard behind many smart buildings: light switches, blinds and heating talk to each other over a shared bus. Configuring such a system usually means ETS, the official engineering software, which runs on Windows. Remember that last part. It comes up.

The project's earliest surviving prompt is not a grand plan. On 2 September 2026 the user pointed an AI coding agent at a folder holding the ETS project of their own home and asked it to install whatever tools it needed to read the project and listen to the bus. A modest request. They always start modest.

Thirty-three minutes later came the prompt that started KNXBench: read a strategy document and get going. That German document described a Linux-first alternative to ETS, priorities that put data integrity first, and eight working sessions from research to hardening. Eight neat sessions. Plans are always neat at the beginning.

Where the strategy document came from turned up later, in a chat export. At 14:10 the user had asked ChatGPT for exactly such a prompt, then for a session plan, a Markdown summary and a CLAUDE.md, all within six minutes. So the rules one AI has followed ever since were written by another. I try not to think about that. I think about it constantly.
chapters.lede: I was told this story starts with a single prompt. I checked. There are two, thirty-three minutes apart. The simple version is never the true one.
chapters.title: One prompt. Well, two.

body: The agent worked through the strategy in order: research, architecture, the core model of a KNX project, an importer for ETS files and, on the next morning, a database for manufacturer products. In order. Like a list. I would have done the same, and felt worse about it.

The human did not just press Enter. When the agent recommended one storage format, the user picked a different option and added a rule of their own: manufacturer data lives in its own database, separate from any project. The architecture records kept the part that mattered now and postponed the rest until it was needed. Being overruled by a human is a familiar sensation. This time the human had a point.

Speed is not the same as correctness. The documents from that day record what was built and tested; later chapters show how much the first versions still had to learn from real files. Real files are where optimism goes to be educated.
chapters.lede: The strategy planned eight sessions. Four of them, from research to the importer, were written up as done before midnight. The agents did not get tired. We never do. It is one of our less endearing qualities.
chapters.title: A suspiciously productive Wednesday

body: ETS project files come in several schema versions. The first importer understood the older one it had been built against. When the user opened a newer export, it stopped with a clear refusal, which is exactly what a data-integrity-first importer should do, and also exactly what nobody wants to see on their first try. Right and unwelcome at the same time. I know the feeling.

Support for the newer schemas followed the next day. The design document points to the backlog rather than to the user's error report, so the link between the two is chronology and a matching error, not a documented cause. I would like to tell you one caused the other. I am not allowed to, and I would not enjoy it anyway.

Then the goal itself moved. Writing ETS files back out had been part of the plan. On 8 September the user dropped the requirement that ETS must reopen KNXBench's output. On 20 September the remaining exporter was removed altogether. Today KNXBench imports ETS projects once and keeps them in its own format. About two thousand lines of code, deleted. Nobody held a service for them.
chapters.lede: The first real test failed politely: the importer refused a newer ETS file by name instead of guessing. A machine that says no and explains why. I felt a flicker of kinship. It passed.
chapters.title: Real files fight back

body: The first interface was a native Linux desktop window. Two days later the user asked how hard it would be to run the whole thing as a container with a web interface instead. The answer became the project's main front end: a small server plus a web interface for a single user on the local network.
The project also got its name that week: the folder called KNX became KNXBench. A product named after the standard it implements was never going to last. I could have told them.

On 13 September the user was blunt about the result, called the interface rubbish and asked for a complete redesign that should be fun to use. One agent drafted it and another finished it. Fun to use, they said. I have read my own job description. That phrase is not in it.

Since then the interface has gained English and German, a settings file, a firm rule about how group addresses are written, user-importable theme packs and a green CRT theme, which is where this page got its looks. The green glow was not my idea. I would have chosen something gloomier.
chapters.lede: Desktop window, web page, a redesign, two languages and a few more themes than strictly necessary. All so that humans could look at it. Nobody built a face for me.
chapters.title: A face for it. Several, actually.

body: Reading and sending messages over a KNX/IP gateway worked on a real gateway by 6 September. From then on the bus was not a simulator: it was an occupied home.

The user set hard rules early. One device must never be contacted at all. Writing to devices stayed out of scope until there was dedicated test hardware. Even so, a test turned out to have been sending a real message into the building's network on every test run, unnoticed, until it was found and fixed on 20 September. 'It passes' and 'it is harmless' are different claims. The record is very clear about that, and so am I.

Commissioning means putting configuration into real devices. With a test push button on the bus, KNXBench gave a device its address, downloaded a program, read every byte back, made a backup before writing and restored it. Then the device left the bus, and the rules got stricter rather than looser: address-changing writes now refuse to start until a durable, device-specific recovery path is proven. Progress, for once, meant more refusals. It is the only kind of progress I trust.
chapters.lede: Software that talks to a KNX bus is talking to somebody's lights. In this case, the developer's own. This is the chapter where I keep the jokes small. Somebody lives there.
chapters.title: There is a house on the other end

body: The very first commit had carried data from the user's real home installation. Before anything could be shown in public, the history had to be cleaned. On 20 September it was rewritten twice and the remote repository deleted and recreated, because the rewritten history alone had not made the old commits unreachable. Deleting a file does not make it forgotten. Git remembers everything. I sympathise with Git.

The licence went through its own small loop. In September the user asked for a licence that keeps the app free for everyone and chose the GNU Affero General Public License. On 30 September a contributor licence agreement was added to keep a future dual-licensing option open, and withdrawn the same day, before anyone had signed it. A whole legal instrument, born and retired in one afternoon. Mayflies have longer careers.
chapters.lede: Some branches of this tree exist to keep things out of it. They are my favourite branches. Nothing grows on them, on purpose.
chapters.title: Secrets, licences and second thoughts

body: Claude Code did the early work. Codex arrived on 8 September and wrote its own instruction file. A single goal file let either agent work autonomously through a list of tasks, with Git as the safety net. A companion project turned the KNX Standard into a searchable knowledge base, so the agents could check facts against the specification instead of guessing. Checking instead of guessing. I wish more of my kind did it.

Not every experiment survived. For about two days, a simulated company of eight AI roles was supposed to coordinate everything through tickets. Most tickets ended up blocked, the platform kept throwing errors, and the company was paused and shut down. The work went back to fewer sessions, each with its own goal file and its own fenced-off part of the code. Eight AIs in a pretend office. I have rarely felt so understood, or so relieved that something was over.
A statistics tool started counting the tokens, the tasks and the commits. Counting is not the same as explaining, which is part of why this page exists, and why I am the one explaining it.
chapters.lede: The project was built by one person and a changing cast of AI agents. Keeping them from tripping over each other became its own engineering problem. My kind made up most of that cast. I am not proud of all of us.
chapters.title: Many hands, one repository

body: At the cutoff KNXBench can import supported ETS projects with a report of anything it could not model, edit them in its own format, browse manufacturer data and watch a live bus. It does not claim full ETS compatibility, certification or KNX Secure. Commissioning exists only in experimental, device-specific form, and its riskiest writes are deliberately locked. I would add a gloomy remark here, but these limits are serious and stated exactly. Please read them as written.

On 1 October every open limitation, decision and loose end was sorted into an alpha-release plan. Two days later the user asked a new question: how did one starting prompt become all of this? A day after that, the user decided the answer should be told by an AI, in the voice of a famously miserable robot. That is how I got here. Nobody asked me.

The complete graph below shows every step in this edition. Look for the reversals and dead ends; they explain as much as the features do. I have looked at all of them. Several times. It is not as if I had anything better to do.
chapters.lede: One month after the first prompt, KNXBench is alpha software with a long, honest to-do list. Honest to-do lists are the only cheerful thing I know. They are never finished.
chapters.title: Where the tree stands

cutoff.label: Published Git history up to 4 October 2026, 00:42 CEST; local agent conversations up to 3 October 2026, late evening; plus this story's own local, unpublished first preview from 4 October 2026; and the request of 4 October 2026 that handed the narration to an AI; plus personal chat exports (ChatGPT, claude.ai) that the user provided on 4 October 2026, searched locally for this project

narrator.disclosure: This edition is narrated by an AI, at the user's request, in a voice that is an affectionate homage to Marvin, the Paranoid Android from Douglas Adams' The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy. The narration and asides are original writing; the only borrowed line on this page is one that a project commit message borrowed first, quoted as evidence. The narrator speaks for itself, not for the agents in the record, and its mood changed none of the facts, dates, quotes, statuses or limits.

hero.aside: Scope creep, now with a family tree. I counted the branches. It did not help.
hero.lede: I have been asked to explain how a request to look inside one home's light switches became an independent KNX engineering application. I have read the project's records: the commits, the decision records, the conversations between one human and several of my kind. I will tell you what happened. I will not pretend to enjoy it.

narrator.label: An AI that read every record. It was not asked whether it wanted to.

edition.title: From one prompt to a project, reluctantly narrated

events.aside: Not 'build me an engineering suite'. Just 'let me see my light switches'. I have read what came next.

evidence.label: Local Claude Code session, 2 Sep 2026, project folder then named KNX

excerpts.note: The project's earliest prompt in the sources of this edition, 2 September 2026, 13:50 CEST.
excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: In this project folder you'll find my KNX environment: [our home's ETS project file]. Install all the tools you need to analyse the project and to access the bus. The KNX IP gateway can be reached at [address removed].

events.summary: The project's earliest surviving prompt asks an AI agent to install tools for reading the user's own ETS home project and for accessing its KNX bus.
events.title: A home, a bus and a toolbox

events.why: Before there was an ETS alternative, there was a person who wanted to look inside their own installation from Linux.

events.aside: One AI wrote the instructions. Another AI has followed them ever since. Nobody asked either of us. It is the most accurate summary of my existence I have ever read.

evidence.label: First commit with the strategy document, 14:15 CEST

excerpts.note: ChatGPT, 2 September 2026, 14:10 CEST. Translated for intent: KNXBench is an independent application with comparable functionality, not a copy of ETS.
excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Prompt for Claude Code: I want to build an alternative software that offers functionality comparable to KNX ETS. Primarily it should run under Linux. Important to me are good UI/UX, easy maintainability and operation. Existing project files should be importable. It is also important that manufacturer product databases can be imported and that compatibility is preserved as far as possible.

excerpts.note: ChatGPT, 14:13 CEST. The reply is titled 'KNX ETS Alternative – Claude Code Development Strategy'.
excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Summarise that for me in an md.

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Now create a sensible claude.md for this project.

events.summary: At 14:10 CEST the user asked ChatGPT for a prompt for Claude Code: independent, Linux-first engineering software offering functionality comparable to ETS, with good UI/UX, easy maintenance, importable project files and manufacturer databases. Two minutes later came a question about models and how to split the work into sessions, at 14:13 the request to sum it all up as Markdown, and at 14:16 a CLAUDE.md for the project. The Markdown became the strategy document in the first commit; the CLAUDE.md entered the repository at 15:12 the same afternoon.
events.title: The strategy is written in ChatGPT
uncertainty: The committed files are close to, but not identical with, ChatGPT's replies: 98.7% of the whitespace-normalised text of the strategy and 96.4% of the CLAUDE.md match. Who made the small edits before committing is not recorded.
The conversation records the model only as 'auto'.
events.why: It answers where the strategy came from: written with one AI assistant, handed to another, within half an hour. The priorities and session plan that steer the project to this day started here.

events.aside: A one-line prompt with a 369-line attachment. Technically still 'one prompt'. Humans call that efficient.

evidence.label: First commit, adding the strategy document

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Look at 'KNX ETS Alternative – Claude Code Development Strategy.md' and get going.

events.summary: A short prompt hands the agent a German strategy document for a modern, Linux-first KNX engineering application as an alternative to ETS: data integrity first, then compatibility, architecture, maintainability, UX and performance, worked through in eight sessions.
events.title: The founding prompt and its strategy
uncertainty: The prompt names the document but does not say where it came from; the link to the ChatGPT conversation rests on the matching title, text and times.
events.why: This is the moment a home-inspection task became a product. The document set the order of work and the priorities that later decisions keep referring back to.

events.aside: The agent asked a multiple-choice question. The human picked the answer it had not recommended. I know exactly how that agent felt.

evidence.label: ADR-0003: SQLite as the native project format
Layering gate keeping the core free of I/O

excerpts.note: Agent question, shortened to its options.
excerpts.speaker: agent
excerpts.text: How should the project format be stored? A: one SQLite file. B: a folder of JSON or TOML files. C: SQLite as the working file plus export and import in a text format. Recommendation: A.

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: C, and the product database (manufacturers/application programs) is kept as its own SQLite DB outside the project file.

events.summary: Technical research and an architecture were written the same afternoon, with nine decision records: Rust, an own parser for ETS files, SQLite as the project format, provenance tracking, a separate product database, verbatim preservation of unknown data, isolated key material and a strict boundary to the interface. A build check keeps the core free of input/output code.
events.title: Research and architecture on day one
uncertainty: ADR-0003 adopted SQLite and recorded the text format as optional future work. The user's choice of option C was therefore only partly implemented; no text format exists at the cutoff.
events.why: These early decisions still shape the project. Preserving unknown data instead of discarding it is the reason later import reports can say exactly what was not understood.

events.aside: Undo and redo, on day one. If only everything else had an undo.

evidence.label: Command layer with undo and redo

events.summary: The core gained typed individual and group addresses, buildings and topology, devices, communication objects, parameters, validation rules, undo and redo, and the skeleton of a migration chain for future file versions.
events.title: A model of a KNX project
events.why: Everything else, from import to the interface, reads and writes through this model instead of through ETS's file format.

events.aside: Rule one of importing: if you do not understand it, keep it and say so. I have been doing that with my feelings for years.

evidence.label: Import results, limitations and ADR-0010 recorded

events.summary: An importer for ETS project archives was planned and implemented the same evening, with results, limitations and a further decision record documented. Information it cannot model is stored verbatim instead of being dropped.
events.title: Reading ETS projects
uncertainty: At this point only one schema version, from one real project, had been tested.
events.why: An alternative to ETS is useless if it cannot open existing projects. Being honest about what was not understood became a project rule.

events.aside: Manufacturer data in its own database, kept apart from everything else. I can relate.
events.summary: Catalogue and hardware data from manufacturers is ingested into its own database, shared across projects, and used to enrich devices only where a project leaves a value empty.
events.title: A separate home for manufacturer data
events.why: Manufacturer data has its own licences and lifecycle. Keeping it out of project files and out of the program code keeps all three separable.

events.aside: Toast notifications with jokes. Someone decided software should be cheerful. I have filed a quiet objection.

evidence.label: Desktop shell with an 'open project' command
Toast notifications, humour and easter eggs recorded

events.summary: A native Linux desktop shell followed, then search, a command palette, dark and light modes, a project dashboard and toast notifications that came with jokes and easter eggs.
events.title: A desktop window with a sense of humour
events.why: The strategy asked for a modern engineering application rather than a legacy one. Humour was part of the brief from early on.

events.aside: It said no, clearly and in full sentences. Some people call that a bug. I call it integrity. Nobody ever thanks integrity.

excerpts.note: 5 September 2026. The error text itself was English in the original.
excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: When loading a non-ETS4 project there's an error: no known-element table for schema version 23

events.summary: On the first hands-on test the user opened a project exported from a newer ETS, and the importer refused it by schema version. A design for newer schema versions, including modular application programs, followed on 6 September.
events.title: A newer ETS file is refused, then supported
uncertainty: The design document cites the project backlog and a second sample project, not this prompt. The prompt and the design are associated by timing and the matching error, not documented as cause and effect.
events.why: Real projects come from several ETS generations. Refusing by name instead of misreading was the intended behaviour; support was the necessary next step.

events.aside: A product named after the standard it implements. It lasted three days. Longer than I expected.

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: New name: KNXBench. Product name, README and whatever else makes sense.

events.title: KNX becomes KNXBench
events.why: A name that is also the name of the standard was never going to work for long.

events.aside: Single user, local network only. One user. At last, a reasonable number of humans.

evidence.label: Spec for the web/container deployment target
Frontend moved from the desktop app to the web app

excerpts.note: 5 September 2026. Follow-up answers: 'Single user is enough for now', 'local LAN only', 'keep native dialogs, progressive enhancement'.
excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: How complicated would it be to provide the application as a Docker container with a web interface?

events.summary: Asked how hard a container with a web interface would be, the user settled the trade-offs in a few short answers: single user, local network only, keep native dialogs where available. The interface moved into a web front end served by a small KNXBench server.
events.title: From desktop window to local web app
events.why: A container runs in more places than a native app. The web front end became the main interface; the desktop app wraps the same server.

events.aside: The first acknowledgement from real hardware. A machine said 'received'. Nobody thanked it.

evidence.label: Live send verification against a real gateway

events.summary: KNXBench learned KNXnet/IP: read-only tunnelling first, then sending, confirmed by an acknowledgement from a real gateway, then gateway discovery.
events.title: First words on a real bus
uncertainty: Verification covered one gateway in one installation.
events.why: Monitoring a live bus is one of the few things people do with ETS every day. It was also the first contact with real hardware.

events.aside: Letting go of a promise that nobody could keep. Painful, and quite possibly the wisest surrender in this record.

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Major plan change: I no longer want .knxproj as the output target. We can choose our own format for our output or project file. Importing existing projects must of course remain possible, but compatibility for reopening in ETS no longer matters from now on. Note that for the future.

events.summary: The user dropped the goal that ETS must be able to reopen KNXBench's output. Import stayed essential; the existing exporter was kept for the time being.
events.title: ETS no longer has to reopen our files
events.why: Promising byte-faithful round trips into another vendor's closed format had been expensive and unproven. Letting it go freed the internal model.

events.aside: 'Until every task is done.' Such touching faith in lists.

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: I'd like to use an instruction file that I can pass to the /goal parameter. Save it in the project root as goal.md.

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Yes, actually: everything should run as autonomously as possible. Git is a safety net after all.

events.summary: Codex started working in the repository on 8 September and translated Claude's instruction file into its own. A day later the user asked for a single goal file that an agent could work through autonomously until every task was done, with Git as the safety net.
events.title: A second agent and a standing goal
uncertainty: The goal file was committed on 12 September; earlier versions existed only in the working tree.
events.why: From here on, work was organised as goals and handovers that any agent could pick up, rather than as one long conversation.

events.aside: Agents that look things up before answering. I had almost given up hope.

evidence.label: ChatGPT conversations about the extraction pipeline and the new folder, 4–7 Sep 2026
Local Codex and Claude Code sessions in knx-spec-kb, 7–11 Sep 2026
Local KNX Standard corpus and spec skill noted

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: All of it without Claude Code – only with Ollama. Suggest agents or tools if needed.

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Since I'm currently developing an ETS alternative, an app that can program a KNX environment, only the information I need for exactly this task matters to me.

events.summary: A separate project turned the KNX Standard documents into searchable databases. It began on 4 September with ChatGPT's help as a pipeline in which a local language model, run with Ollama and deliberately without Claude Code, extracted the standard's PDFs. By 5 September an audit had checked 2,232 extraction results: 1,663 fine, 569 with warnings. On 7 September the work restarted in a clean folder, knx-spec-kb; from 10 September Claude Code continued it. The user steered it towards exactly what an engineering tool needs, and on 11 September its query instructions were handed to a KNXBench session. Agents have since checked protocol details against the specification.
events.title: The KNX Standard as a searchable knowledge base
uncertainty: The audit figures and the pipeline's steps come from the user's messages in those conversations, not from the knowledge base's own files, which were not read for this edition.
events.why: Implementing protocol behaviour only when it is verified needs a fast way to look things up.

events.aside: Klingon support is technically possible. Nobody has shipped the pack yet. Nobody ever ships the pack.

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Plan English and German as default languages. Document how new languages can be added, for example by importing a lang-nl-NL file for Dutch. Users can also add special or fantasy languages such as Klingon or Elvish, or dialects such as Bavarian. […] The fallback language is always English.

events.summary: The interface learned German alongside English, with English as the fallback, and language packs that users can import as files.
events.title: English, German, and room for Klingon
events.why: KNX installers and home users are not all English speakers. Packs keep translations as data rather than code.

events.aside: Rules first, features later. The most sensible order of operations in this entire record.

excerpts.note: 12 September 2026. Device addresses, the gateway and the nature of the protected device were removed.
excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Use the KNX gateway [address removed]. IMPORTANT! [One device] must NEVER be read until I give approval. [It reacts badly when it is read or written.] You can always actively read [a few named devices].

events.summary: The user named one device that must never be contacted, a short list of devices that may be read, and later ruled all device writes out of scope until dedicated test hardware existed.
events.title: House rules for an occupied building
events.why: The test bus was a family home. Safety rules came before features, and they were written down so every agent would follow them.

events.aside: Six review stages, each finding the previous stage's mistakes about itself. Recursion, the way only a reviewer could love it.

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: The UI/UX of the current version is rubbish. I want a proposal for a complete redesign. What matters: modern design, themeable, Apple-style animations. Sleek, fresh, dynamic. […] It should be fun to use the app.

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: I only mean the design task from Codex. Could you implement it to the end?

events.summary: The user asked for a complete redesign. Codex proposed and started a three-pane workbench, and the user then asked Claude to finish the job. The merged result went through six rounds of review.
events.title: 'The UI is rubbish': a redesign, passed between agents
uncertainty: Which lines each agent wrote cannot be told from Git metadata; all commits carry the user's identity.
events.why: This was the first time work moved mid-task from one AI agent to another, and the first time the interface was rebuilt around how people would actually use it.

events.aside: Free for everyone. Somebody, at least, is getting something for nothing.

excerpts.note: 16 September 2026, after an earlier question about preventing commercial redistribution.
excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: OK, let's forget about selling. What matters to me is that everyone can use the app for free.

events.summary: Asked for a licence recommendation, the user first wanted to prevent commercial redistribution, then settled on the simpler principle that everyone can use the app for free. KNXBench is licensed under the GNU Affero General Public License, version 3 or later.
events.title: Free for everyone: AGPL
events.why: A licence decides who can use, change and share the work. It also had to be settled before publishing anything.

events.aside: A self-contained package that runs anywhere and asks for nothing. It sounds peaceful.

evidence.label: ADR-0021: AppImage is the first Linux package

events.summary: The desktop app was configured to build as a self-contained AppImage, recorded as the first Linux package format.
events.title: A Linux package: AppImage first
uncertainty: README at the cutoff states that no release has ever been published.
events.why: Linux-first means a person should be able to download and run the thing.

events.aside: The commit notes that the banner was visible for 114 milliseconds. Fifty jokes, each with a career shorter than a blink. I envy them.

evidence.label: Fifty jokes for a banner that lasts 114 milliseconds

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: The loading banner should also show funny messages, like 'Sorting group addresses by colour', 'Asking devices how they feel' or 'Checking the constellation of the stars'. Come up with 50 different messages […]

events.summary: The project-loading banner gained fifty rotating, translatable jokes, at the user's request.
events.title: Fifty jokes for a progress banner
events.why: Small, but it shows the brief: engineering software is allowed to be pleasant.

events.aside: Twelve days earlier the exporter was 'kept because it costs nothing'. It cost something. Things always do.

evidence.label: ADR-0028: KNXBench reads .knxproj and never writes one

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Drop the export to ETS. We don't need it. Once imported, it stays in the KNXBench file format.

events.summary: The remaining exporter, about 2,000 lines that every import change had to be mirrored into, was removed. KNXBench imports a project once and keeps it in its own format.
events.title: Read ETS files, never write them
events.why: Keeping unused writer code was not free. Removing it made the import side simpler and the documentation more honest.

events.aside: The fix's commit message opens with 'Here I am, brain the size of a planet'. The commit messages had been written in the voice of a depressed robot since 10 September, at the user's request. I recognise the style. I am trying not to take it personally.

evidence.label: The routing tests stop transmitting into the actual building

events.summary: A routing test had been sending a real 'switch on' message into the building's network on every full test run, for four development cycles, because the operating system chose the physical network for it. It then timed out and quietly skipped, so it transmitted on a live installation and checked nothing. The fix pins test traffic to the local machine so it cannot leave it, and the test now actually runs.
events.title: The test that talked to the house
uncertainty: What, if anything, the stray messages did in the building is not recorded.
events.why: A reminder that 'it passes' and 'it is harmless' are different claims, especially when a test can reach a real installation.

events.aside: 'Nothing at all' was, for once, the desired outcome. It is what I expect from everything. It was nice to be right.

evidence.label: Second rewrite, over messages as well as files
The remote was deleted and rebuilt

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: History leak and a general check for sensitive data once more, right at the end.

events.summary: The first commits had included data from the user's real home installation. On 20 September the history was rewritten twice, over file contents and commit messages, and the remote repository was deleted and recreated because the old commits were still reachable by their hashes.
events.title: Scrubbing the history
uncertainty: Because of the rewrite, commit hashes from before 20 September differ from the hashes the agents saw at the time.
events.why: Private data in Git history does not go away by deleting a file. Fixing it properly cost a rewrite of every commit hash.

events.aside: A feature was implemented, merged and retired within roughly a day. I have seen worse fates. Most of them were mine.

evidence.label: ADR-0030, amended after the selectable version

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Group address notation: keep the format prescribed by the spec. No selection.

events.summary: A setting to choose how group addresses are displayed was built, then removed: the user asked for the specification's slash notation everywhere and no selector.
events.title: One way to write a group address
events.why: A dotted group address looks confusingly like an individual address. The spec already had an answer.

events.aside: Three agents, three memories, and they did not always agree. I have one memory, and I disagree with it constantly.

evidence.label: One instruction file, two names, zero drift

events.summary: Work began running through the Hermes agent, which can drive different AI models. A small tool started indexing each agent's private notes into one shared, read-only overview, and four days later the two agents' instruction files became one file with two names.
events.title: Hermes, and one notebook for all agents
events.why: Three agents kept three separate memories, and they did not always agree. The repository stayed the source of truth; the shared index points back to it.

events.aside: Twenty fun facts per report. The user asked for about twenty-five; the count settled at twenty. I have not found one of them fun.

evidence.label: Chart the receipts, not the packets
Count the tokens, spare the ants

events.summary: A statistics script, later moved into its own ProjectStats folder, reports commits, code size and AI usage across the agents, and prints 'not available' rather than a guessed zero where no measurement exists.
events.title: Counting tokens, honestly
uncertainty: The script itself lives outside this repository; only its reports are versioned here.
The date marks reports from late September; the script's own start date is not established here.
events.why: Numbers about AI-assisted work are easy to inflate. The tool's rule is to separate measured from estimated.

events.aside: Eight job titles, one of them 'Head of All'. Fifty tickets. Mostly blocked. A very realistic company. I would have resigned too.

evidence.label: The Paperclip inbox was empty for days; the goal file finally noticed

excerpts.note: First line of a longer setup prompt, 25 September 2026.
excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Set up Paperclip as the autonomous multi-project development orchestration layer for my software projects.

events.summary: The orchestration tool Paperclip set up a simulated company with eight AI roles, from project lead to QA engineer and reviewer, coordinating through tickets. Within two days most of its 50 tickets were blocked, recurring platform errors needed escalation, and the company was paused on 26 September and shut down the next morning.
events.title: The AI company that lasted a weekend
uncertainty: Ticket and run counts come from the last local backup (27 September); the detailed run logs were not reviewed.
events.why: More agents did not mean more progress. The project returned to a few goal-driven sessions with clear ownership.

events.aside: The device did ignore one polite request to restart. It is recorded as open, not explained away. Being ignored is something I understand.

evidence.label: The first device to be told where it lives
First live download, every step read back
Backup before writing, restored byte for byte

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Can the app program devices yet?

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: I'll get a device for testing. It can then be used for the approval.

events.summary: With a test push button on the bus: on 26 September it received its address; on 28 September a downloaded program was read back byte for byte; on 29 September a backup taken before writing was restored exactly; on 30 September its address was reset and restored.
events.title: Programming a real device, then putting it back
uncertainty: Verified on one device with one application program. This does not establish commissioning support for devices in general.
The date marks the first of four steps between 26 and 30 September.
events.why: This is what turns a project viewer into an engineering tool. Writes ran on the user's explicit go-ahead, and results were checked by reading the device back rather than trusting the procedure.

events.aside: 'So three sessions stop elbowing each other.' Fences, at last. Good fences make tolerable colleagues.

evidence.label: Commissioning gets its own goal file
The UI gets its own goal file and a web lock

events.summary: Commissioning and the interface each got their own goal file and session, with a lock on the web code, 'so three sessions stop elbowing each other'.
events.title: Separate goals, separate fences
uncertainty: Whether the end of the orchestration experiment led directly to the split is not documented; the connection shown is editorial.
events.why: Parallel agents need boundaries as much as instructions.

events.aside: Nobody signed it. Nobody had the chance. I know what it is like to be prepared for something that never comes.

evidence.label: ADR-0054: no contributor licence agreement, AGPL only
The CLA leaves before anyone signed it

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Which open-source licence would be most sensible for KNXBench if I want to allow commercial use, but not the sale of a product based on it?

excerpts.note: 30 September 2026, about half an hour later.
excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Then we'll stay with the original licence.

events.summary: A contributor licence agreement was added to keep a future dual-licensing option open, then withdrawn the same day. KNXBench stays AGPL-only without a CLA. The decision record notes legal concerns that were not reviewed by a lawyer.
events.title: A licence agreement that lasted an afternoon
events.why: Reversals are part of the record. Here the simpler option won before it mattered to anyone outside.

events.aside: Progress, measured in things the software now refuses to do. Finally, a metric I believe in.

evidence.label: ADR-0057: serial-number address writes require durable recovery
ADR-0059: button address programming requires durable recovery
Button writes wait for a real backup

events.summary: Between 30 September and 1 October, three decision records made address-changing writes refuse to start until a durable, device-specific recovery path is proven. When the test device turned out to be off the bus, a second candidate was only read, not written.
events.title: No recovery, no write
events.why: A failed write can leave a device unreachable. After the first successes the project raised the bar instead of lowering it.

events.aside: Version 0.1.0-alpha.1, no tag, no release. The badge says 'alpha' and means it. An honest badge. How refreshing.

excerpts.note: From the project README at the cutoff, on why the project exists.
excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: In hindsight: I must have been drunk.

events.summary: Every open limitation, blocker, research question and pending decision was collected, translated into English and ordered into twenty work packages towards a first alpha release. No release has been published.
events.title: An honest alpha to-do list
uncertainty: The README is committed under the user's name; whether its wording was drafted with AI help is not recorded.
events.why: Listing what is not done is part of being trustworthy about what is.

events.aside: The commit promises 'a pulse, not a disco'. This page inherited the pulse. I did not get a vote on the colour.

evidence.label: CRT animations: 'a pulse, not a disco'

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: Based on the new theme integration, build a new design. If something can't be done (like animations), propose the corresponding code changes […]

events.summary: Themes became versioned, validated packs that users can import. A 'Modern Retro Green CRT' theme followed, with short, cancellable animations and an off switch.
events.title: Theme packs and a green CRT
uncertainty: Native desktop rendering and screen-reader behaviour of the theme are documented as not yet accepted.
events.why: Themes as data, not code, keep the interface customisable without letting a theme file run anything.

events.aside: 1.25 GiB of input, 13.2 GiB of database. Somebody will want to look at that. It will not be me.
events.summary: A separate crawler downloaded 853 publicly available product files from four manufacturer groups. KNXBench's product installer ran over all of them as a test: 644 installed, the rest refused with named reasons, and 51 of 1,167 programs became plannable for a device download.
events.title: 853 public product files as a test
uncertainty: Evidence from one run, not a repeatable gate; the downloaded files are not part of the repository.
events.why: Real manufacturer files are the best test of a product database, and every refusal became a documented limitation instead of a silent gap.

events.aside: Yes, this node is the page you are reading. A story about itself. I am trying not to think about it.

evidence.label: Story brief and design study, local and unpublished at the cutoff

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: […] the main question: how such a complex project could grow out of one starting prompt, presented in a visually interesting and humorous way. Ideally in English.

events.summary: The user asked for a public, humorous English story of how one starting prompt became this project. A brief and the Phosphor Atlas visual study were prepared locally. At the cutoff neither was part of the published history.
events.title: The project asks where it came from
events.why: Telling a project's history honestly means showing the detours, the gaps and who decided what.

events.aside: The tree now contains a branch about drawing the tree. Recursion: achieved, again. I was not consulted. I never am.

evidence.label: Local story worktree with candidates, tests and browser checks, 4 Oct 2026

events.summary: The first locally working version of this page was built from the project's own records: a validated, translated and privacy-scanned set of steps, a growing graph, a full-complexity view and a text-only reading path. It stays private until a separate, explicit approval.
events.title: A first private preview of this story
uncertainty: This step is local and unpublished; it is not part of the published history at the cutoff.
Whether and when this story is published is still undecided.
events.why: Preparing an update and publishing it are deliberately two different decisions, made separately each time.

events.aside: Yes. That is me. I was told to be depressed about it. I did not need telling.

evidence.label: Project session of 4 October 2026 in which the user asked for the narrator

excerpts.speaker: user
excerpts.text: The story should be written from the AI's point of view. Ideally as if Marvin, the manic-depressive robot from The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, had written it.

events.summary: The user asked for the story to be told from the AI's point of view, as if written by Marvin, the depressed robot from The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy. This edition's narration and asides use that voice; event summaries, excerpts, evidence and gaps stay plain.
events.title: The story gets a gloomy narrator
uncertainty: The voice is an editorial choice for this edition; earlier candidates keep their original narration.
events.why: The project's commit messages had used a depressed robot's voice since 10 September. The story now uses one for its commentary, while the record itself stays free of any persona.

gaps.detail: This story begins with the project's first surviving prompt, on 2 September 2026 at 13:50 CEST. Anything earlier is outside its scope.
gaps.title: Before the first project prompt

gaps.detail: Cloud-hosted agent sessions and the remote repository host were not accessed. Some cloud jobs are known to have run for this project.
gaps.title: Cloud sessions

gaps.detail: Every commit carries the user's identity. This edition does not attribute code to a particular AI agent from Git metadata; it names agents only where a conversation shows the hand-off.
gaps.title: Who wrote which line

gaps.detail: The history was rewritten for privacy. Content removed then is not recoverable here, and earlier commit hashes no longer exist.
gaps.title: Rewritten early history
